# Āḷavaka Sutta (Snp 1.10 (PTS Snp 31))
**ID:** Snp 1.10 (PTS Snp 31)
**Section:** Suttanipāta (snp)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Āḷavaka Sutta
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/snp1.10
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0505m.mul0.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Āḷavaka Sutta* (Snp 1.10) is the tenth discourse in the *Uragavagga*, the opening section of the *Suttanipāta* [SuttaCentral; Sutherland 1991]. Set in the haunt of the *yakkha* Āḷavaka near the town of Āḷavī, the narrative depicts an initial challenge wherein the spirit repeatedly commands the Buddha to exit and re-enter his dwelling [Sutherland 1991; Saddhatissa 2013]. When the Buddha declines to leave on the fourth demand, the *yakkha* threatens to scatter his mind, rip open his heart, or fling him across the River Ganges unless he successfully answers his riddles [SuttaCentral; Sutherland 1991]. The ensuing dialogue employs an *ākhyāna* (ballad) question-and-answer form drawing on ancient Indian gnomic poetry, highlighting themes of ethical conduct, wisdom, and lay morality—notably praising truth (*sacca*), virtue (*dhamma*), resolve (*dhiti*), and generosity (*cāga*) [Piya Tan 2004; Kalupahana 2001; Anandajoti 2010]. In early Buddhist narrative, the conversion of Āḷavaka exemplifies the motif of the reluctant, skeptical demon subdued by the transformative power of the Dhamma [Buswell 2004].
In practical and ritual contexts, the discourse is chanted as a protective text (*paritta*) credited with imparting mental composure and moral purity, and it forms part of the extended *Catubhāṇavārapāḷi* recension [Kalupahana 2001; Analayo 2018]. The sutta shares an identical canonical counterpart in the *Saṁyutta Nikāya* (*Yakkha Saṁyutta*, SN 10.12) as well as close structural parallels with the *Sūciloma Sutta* (Snp 2.5 / SN 10.3) [SuttaCentral; Sutherland 1991; Saddhatissa 2013]. DharmaNexus matches confirm this extensive Pali-internal reuse, recording direct correspondence between Snp 1.10 (§0.1–17.4) and SN 10.12 (§12.0.3–12.13.4), as well as textual overlap with the *Suttanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* and Snp 2.5 [DharmaNexus]. Outside Pali, SuttaCentral lists full parallels in Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* collections (SA 1326, SA 603, and SA2 325), alongside verse-level parallels in the *Śarīrārthagāthā*, the *Udānavarga* (*Śraddhāvarga*), and Chinese Dharmapada texts (T 210, T 212, T 213) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus independently reflects cross-linguistic alignment with the Chinese *Za ahan jing* (T 99) and *Bieyi za ahan jing* (T 100), as well as sections of the Tibetan *Vinayavibhaṅga* (D 3-4) and *Udānavarga* (D 326) [DharmaNexus]. A later Central Asian adaptation also survives in fragments of the Old Uygur *Daśakarmapathāvadānamālā* (*Ātavakāvadāna*), although its narrative elements diverge significantly from the Pali transmission [Elverskog 1997].
